_about: Single source of truth for every date in the app. Standard textbook figures. Early-universe events use tAfter (years after the Big Bang) because 13.8e9 minus a microsecond is not representable as 'years ago'. Later events use tAgo (years before today). Ranges are [low, high] in the same unit. Sources: NASA/WMAP/Planck summaries for cosmology; standard geological time scale (ICS 2023) for Earth history; CE years relative to presentYear.

events.label: Big Bang
events.note: About 13.8 billion years ago. Time, space and the hot dense soup begin.

events.label: First protons and neutrons
events.note: About one microsecond after the Big Bang, quarks bind into protons and neutrons.

events.label: First nuclei (H, He)
events.note: About 3 to 20 minutes after the Big Bang. Roughly 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass.

events.label: First light (CMB)
events.note: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, electrons bind to nuclei and the universe becomes transparent. This light is the cosmic microwave background.

events.label: First stars
events.note: About 100 to 200 million years after the Big Bang. The exact time is uncertain.

events.label: Milky Way's oldest stars
events.note: About 13 billion years ago.

events.label: A smaller galaxy merges in (Gaia-Enceladus)
events.note: About 11 to 10 billion years ago a smaller galaxy fell into the young Milky Way; its scattered stars were identified in Gaia data in 2018.

events.label: Thin disk settles
events.note: The thin disk, where the Sun lives, is conventionally dated to about 10 to 8 billion years ago; a puffier thick disk formed earlier, from about 13 billion years ago. Debated: a 2024 Gaia study suggests the thin disk may be much older.

events.label: Sun forms
events.note: About 4.57 billion years ago.

events.label: Earth forms
events.note: About 4.54 billion years ago.

events.label: Moon-forming impact
events.note: About 4.5 billion years ago a Mars-sized body, Theia, is thought to have struck the young Earth.

events.label: Oldest minerals hint at liquid water
events.note: Zircon crystals about 4.4 billion years old suggest liquid water already existed.

events.label: Late heavy bombardment
events.note: About 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago. Whether it was a distinct spike is debated.

events.label: Earliest accepted evidence of life
events.note: Stromatolites about 3.5 billion years ago. Earlier claims (about 3.7 billion years) are debated.

events.label: Great Oxidation Event
events.note: About 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen starts to build up in the atmosphere. The rise plays out over a few hundred million years (to about 2.0 billion years ago) and levels stay far below today's.

events.label: First complex (eukaryotic) cells
events.note: About 2.0 to 1.6 billion years ago.

events.label: Oxygen rises toward today's level
events.note: About 800 to 540 million years ago (the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event), oxygen climbs toward modern levels, setting the stage for large animals. Its timing and size are still debated.

events.label: Snowball Earth
events.note: About 720 to 635 million years ago, ice may have covered most of the planet.

events.label: Cambrian explosion
events.note: About 539 million years ago, most major animal groups appear in the fossil record.

events.label: First land plants
events.note: About 470 million years ago.

events.label: First four-legged animals
events.note: About 365 million years ago; they still lived mostly in water. Tiktaalik (about 375 million years ago) was a fish with limb-like fins; trackways near 390 million years old are debated.

events.label: End-Permian extinction
events.note: About 252 million years ago. Roughly 90% of marine species were lost.

events.label: First dinosaurs
events.note: About 230 million years ago.

events.label: First mammals
events.note: About 225 to 200 million years ago.

events.label: End-Cretaceous extinction
events.note: 66 million years ago an asteroid impact ends the age of dinosaurs (except birds). Roughly 75% of species were lost.

events.label: Human and chimpanzee lineages split
events.note: About 8 to 6 million years ago (estimates vary); Sahelanthropus, one of the earliest hominins, is about 7 million years old.

events.label: Genus Homo
events.note: About 2.8 million years ago.

events.label: Controlled use of fire
events.note: About 1 million years ago, possibly earlier; habitual use is clear by about 400,000 years ago. Debated.

events.label: Homo sapiens
events.note: About 300,000 years ago.

events.label: Earliest known cave art
events.note: About 51,000 to 45,000 years ago (Sulawesi, Indonesia). Older claims are debated.

events.label: Agriculture
events.note: About 12,000 years ago.

events.label: Writing
events.note: About 5,200 years ago.

events.label: Industrial revolution
events.note: Around 1760 CE.

events.label: First human in space
events.note: 1961: Yuri Gagarin.

events.label: Today
events.note: Now.
